## Previously

In Capstone Project 2, you fit a molecular clock to a tree of 24 SARS-CoV-2
genomes

. . .

I estimated that tree with a program called IQ-TREE, on my computer

. . .

::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
Could ***you*** redo the whole analysis, from the genomes to the clock?
Could ***I*** redo it a year from now?
:::

::: {.notes}
0:00-1:30

The capstone handed them a tree. Ask: what would you need from me to make that
tree yourself? (The data, the program, the right version of it, the exact
command, the settings.) That list is today's topic.
:::

## Will it run next year?

A true story from October 2026:

::: {style="font-size: 85%;"}
1.  A command that set up a marimo notebook worked fine in September
2.  In October, ***the same command*** failed with a long error message
3.  Nothing about the notebook had changed
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 85%;"}
What changed? **Python 3.15** was released.
The command asked for "the newest Python," and one of marimo's
dependencies didn't work with 3.15 yet
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
Software changes under your feet, even when your code doesn't
:::

::: {.notes}
1:30-3:00

This happened while I was preparing the course materials (pixi's notebook
sandbox picked Python 3.15, and marimo's `loro` dependency had no build for
3.15 yet). The fix was one line: ask for Python 3.14 specifically. That's
the idea behind everything today: write down exactly what you need.
:::

## A reproducibility problem

In a survey of 1,576 researchers:^[@Baker2016]

::: {.incremental}
-   More than **70%** had tried and failed to reproduce ***another***
    scientist's experiments
-   More than **50%** had failed to reproduce ***their own***
:::

. . .

Computational work ***should*** be the easy case: a computer does the same
thing every time, if we give it the same data, code, software, and steps

::: {.notes}
3:00-4:00

Most of the survey is about wet-lab work, where reproducing results is
genuinely hard. Computational results should be perfectly reproducible, but
in practice they often aren't, because people don't record enough.
:::

## What we need to record

::: {style="font-size: 75%;"}
| Ingredient | Example | How we'll record it |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Data** | The 24 aligned genomes | Record how we got it (and a copy if it's not huge) |
| **Code** | `clock.py` | ***git*** |
| **Software** | Python 3.14, NumPy, IQ-TREE, ... | ***pixi*** |
| **Steps** | The exact IQ-TREE command | ***pixi tasks*** |
| **Randomness** | IQ-TREE's random search | A ***seed*** |
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 85%;"}
See @Sandve2013 and @Wilson2017 for more good habits
:::

::: {.notes}
4:00-5:00

This table is the whole lecture. Everything else is how to do each row.
:::

# Version control with git {background-color="#1b3a5c"}

## Without version control

::: {style="font-size: 160%;"}
```
clock.py
clock_v2.py
clock_v2_fixed.py
clock_FINAL.py
clock_FINAL_omicron_removed_USE_THIS_ONE.py
```
:::

. . .

-   Which version made Figure 2?
-   What changed between them?
-   What if I delete the wrong one?

::: {.notes}
5:00-6:00

Everyone has done this. Ask who has a "final_final" file somewhere.
:::

## Git keeps a history of snapshots

A ***commit*** is a snapshot of your files, with a message, an author, and a
date

::: {style="font-size: 112%;"}
```
$ git log --oneline
36c37de Leave Omicron out of the clock
2fc175a Add the molecular clock script and task
99de975 Estimate the ML tree with IQ-TREE
f9d8d06 Add task to download the SARS-CoV-2 alignment, and the data
3d7a7c5 Add IQ-TREE from bioconda
f2f0520 Create a pixi environment with Python 3.14
12f7a96 Add project title and author to README
539e886 Initial commit
```
:::

. . .

One file name, and every version of it, forever

::: {.notes}
6:00-7:00

This is the history you'll build in the exercise. The hex codes are hashes:
unique IDs for each snapshot. Good commit messages say what changed, so the
log reads like a lab notebook.
:::

## Making a commit

```{=html}
<div style="display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center; gap: 0.3em; font-size: 0.75em; margin: 0.5em 0;">
<div style="border: 3px solid #1b3a5c; border-radius: 10px; padding: 0.35em 0.6em; text-align: center; background: #eef3f8; line-height: 1.2;">Your files<br><span style="font-size: 70%;">working folder</span></div>
<div style="text-align: center; line-height: 1.1;"><code style="font-size: 70%; white-space: nowrap;">git add</code><br><span style="font-size: 150%;">&#10230;</span></div>
<div style="border: 3px solid #1b3a5c; border-radius: 10px; padding: 0.35em 0.6em; text-align: center; background: #eef3f8; line-height: 1.2;">Staged<br><span style="font-size: 70%;">changes</span></div>
<div style="text-align: center; line-height: 1.1;"><code style="font-size: 70%; white-space: nowrap;">git commit</code><br><span style="font-size: 150%;">&#10230;</span></div>
<div style="border: 3px solid #1b3a5c; border-radius: 10px; padding: 0.35em 0.6em; text-align: center; background: #eef3f8; line-height: 1.2;">Your history<br><span style="font-size: 70%;">.git folder</span></div>
<div style="text-align: center; line-height: 1.1;"><code style="font-size: 70%; white-space: nowrap;">git push</code><br><span style="font-size: 150%;">&#10230;</span></div>
<div style="border: 3px solid #1b3a5c; border-radius: 10px; padding: 0.35em 0.6em; text-align: center; background: #eef3f8; line-height: 1.2;">GitHub<br><span style="font-size: 70%;">backup &amp; sharing</span></div>
</div>
```

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 85%;"}
-   ***Stage*** (`git add`) chooses which changes go in the next snapshot
-   ***Commit*** (`git commit -m "message"`) saves the snapshot
-   ***Push*** (`git push`) backs it up on GitHub, where others can see it
:::

::: {.notes}
7:00-8:30

The staging step is the one people find odd. It lets you make several changes
and commit them as separate, meaningful snapshots. `git status` tells you which
box each change is in; run it constantly.
:::

## Everyday git

::: {style="font-size: 80%;"}
| Command | What it does |
|:--|:--|
| `git status` | What has changed since my last commit? |
| `git diff <file>` | ***Exactly*** what changed, line by line |
| `git add <file>` | Stage a file's changes for the next commit |
| `git commit -m "..."` | Save a snapshot of the staged changes |
| `git push` | Send my commits to GitHub |
| `git log --oneline` | List my commits |
| `git restore <file>` | Undo changes since my last commit |
:::

::: {.notes}
8:30-9:30

These seven commands cover almost everything you'll do with git in this course.
:::

## What to commit

::: {style="font-size: 80%;"}
| Commit it | Don't commit it |
|:--|:--|
| Code and scripts | Installed software (`.pixi/`) |
| The instructions for the software (`pixi.toml`, `pixi.lock`) | Files that change every run (logs with dates) |
| Small data, and where it came from | Big data (record how to get it instead) |
| Key results (the tree, the figure) | Temporary files |
:::

. . .

A `.gitignore` file lists what git should ignore

::: {.notes}
9:30-10:30

Rule of thumb: commit what you can't easily recreate, plus small results you
want to compare between versions. Big data goes in a public archive (like
GenBank), and the repository records how to download it.
:::

# Reproducible environments with pixi {background-color="#1b3a5c"}

## "It works on my computer"

Our analysis needs Python, NumPy, SciPy, matplotlib, and IQ-TREE

. . .

Each of those needs other packages, which need other packages, ...

. . .

::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
Each one has a version, and a different version can change your results, or
break your code
:::

::: {.notes}
10:30-11:30

In the exercise, `pixi list` will show how many packages are really in the
environment (many more than the five we ask for).
:::

## A project environment

```{=html}
<div style="display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center; gap: 0.3em; font-size: 0.75em; margin: 0.5em 0;">
<div style="border: 3px solid #1b3a5c; border-radius: 10px; padding: 0.35em 0.6em; text-align: center; background: #eef3f8; line-height: 1.2;"><code>pixi.toml</code><br><span style="font-size: 70%;">what we asked for</span></div>
<div style="text-align: center; line-height: 1.1;"><code style="font-size: 70%; white-space: nowrap;">pixi solves</code><br><span style="font-size: 150%;">&#10230;</span></div>
<div style="border: 3px solid #1b3a5c; border-radius: 10px; padding: 0.35em 0.6em; text-align: center; background: #eef3f8; line-height: 1.2;"><code>pixi.lock</code><br><span style="font-size: 70%;">exactly what we got</span></div>
<div style="text-align: center; line-height: 1.1;"><code style="font-size: 70%; white-space: nowrap;">pixi install</code><br><span style="font-size: 150%;">&#10230;</span></div>
<div style="border: 3px solid #1b3a5c; border-radius: 10px; padding: 0.35em 0.6em; text-align: center; background: #eef3f8; line-height: 1.2;"><code>.pixi/</code><br><span style="font-size: 70%;">the installed software</span></div>
</div>
```

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 85%;"}
-   **Commit** `pixi.toml` and `pixi.lock`: small text files
-   **Don't commit** `.pixi/`: big, and pixi can rebuild it, ***exactly***,
    from the lock file
:::

::: {.notes}
11:30-13:00

The manifest says "Python 3.14, any NumPy 2." The lock file says "Python
3.14.x, NumPy 2.y.z, and these 70-odd other packages, downloaded from these
exact addresses." Anyone with the lock file gets the same environment.
:::

## Building an environment

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
pixi init
pixi add "python=3.14.*" numpy scipy matplotlib marimo
pixi workspace channel add bioconda
pixi add iqtree
```

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 80%;"}
-   Packages come from ***channels***: [conda-forge](https://conda-forge.org/)
    (general scientific software) and [bioconda](https://bioconda.github.io/)
    (bioinformatics)
-   They include programs that ***aren't Python***, like IQ-TREE
    (molab can only install Python packages)
-   `"python=3.14.*"` pins the version we care about
:::

::: {.notes}
13:00-14:30

conda (and its faster cousins mamba and pixi) all use the same channels.
pixi adds lock files and tasks, and keeps each environment inside its project
folder.
:::

## Recording the steps: tasks

A ***task*** saves a command in `pixi.toml`, so anyone can rerun it

::: {style="font-size: 120%;"}
```{.toml filename="pixi.toml (simplified)"}
[tasks]
get-data = "curl -L -o data/sars-cov-2.fasta https://..."
tree = "iqtree3 -s data/sars-cov-2.fasta -m HKY -seed 1 ..."
clock = { cmd = "python scripts/clock.py", depends-on = ["tree"] }
```
:::

. . .

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
pixi run clock
```

One command runs the whole analysis, from the alignment to the figure

::: {.notes}
14:30-16:00

(pixi will also add a description to each task in the exercise.) `-seed 1`
fixes IQ-TREE's random numbers, so it finds exactly the same tree every time.
Without a seed, IQ-TREE picks one from the clock, and the branch lengths can
differ slightly between runs. In the exercise you'll try seed 2 and use git to
see what changed.
:::

# The exercise {background-color="#1b3a5c"}

## Codespaces

A ***codespace*** is a Linux computer in the cloud, which you use in your web
browser, with git and pixi already installed

. . .

::: {.callout-warning appearance="minimal"}
Codespaces are ***temporary***: GitHub deletes a codespace after 30 days
without use, even if your work isn't pushed. **Commit and push often!**
:::

::: {.notes}
16:00-17:00

They have free hours each month (more with GitHub's student benefits). Stop
the codespace when you're done to save hours.
:::

## The real test

At the end of the exercise, you will:

::: {.incremental}
1.  ***Delete*** your codespace
2.  Make a brand new one from your GitHub repository
3.  Run `pixi run clock`
4.  Run `git status`
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 160%;"}
```
nothing to commit, working tree clean
```
:::

The new computer reproduced your tree and figure, ***exactly***

::: {.notes}
17:00-18:00

This is the payoff. If every byte of the tree and the figure matches what
they committed, git has nothing to report.
:::

## The plan

::: {style="font-size: 85%;"}
1.  **Your project repository**: Make your copy, and your first commit
2.  **A reproducible environment**: Python, packages, and IQ-TREE with pixi
3.  **Estimating the tree**: IQ-TREE as a pixi task; what to commit
4.  **Fitting the clock**: Change the analysis; go back in time with git;
    why the seed matters
5.  **Prove it's reproducible**: Delete, rebuild, rerun
:::

. . .

Each part ends with a push, so you can stop after any part

::: {.notes}
18:00-19:00

Each part is about 30 to 45 minutes; we'll do this over a few class periods.
:::
